submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole fires on words and phrases that assign or allot something to a place, use, role or status: designate/designation (strongest, in every inflection and in its translations such as 指定), assign, allocate, allot, apportion, earmark, 'set aside', and more weakly appoint, nominate and delegate. It tracks that meaning rather than a token or word form (the object being assigned is irrelevant: 'designated driver', 'designated hitter' and 'designated the room for the hearings' fire as hard as 'designated a UNESCO site'), while give/transfer verbs (gave, handed, transferred, grant, award, donate), divide verbs (distribute, divide, share) and naming verbs (call, name, label, dub, term, classify, declare) stay quiet.

rival_explanations: Broader reading: the pole marks any verb that transfers or confers a resource or status (grant, award, donate, transfer, distribute, divide, share), so the allocation verbs are only its commonest case and it should fire on 'The funds were donated to the school' and 'They divided the profit among the heirs'.

Narrower reading: only the English lemma designate/designation and its direct translations are the real trigger, and the allocation verbs are incidental co-firings, so the pole should not fire in new text on allocate, allot, apportion, earmark or 'set aside'.

Are there any other notable documentaries that will be shown at the Hot Docs festival besides those included in the Special Presentations sidebar?: The Special Presentations sidebar is likely to generate heat with Dawn Porter's 'Trapped' and Stephanie Soechtig's 'Under the Gun,' executive produced by Katie Couric.
A slew of documentaries on gun culture, abortion and climate change were unveiled Tuesday by the Hot Docs Canadian International Documentary Festival for its Special Presentations sidebar.
These include international premieres for Dawn Porter's Trapped, the Sundance jury award winner about legal challenges to U.S. Abortion clinics, and Stephanie Soechtig's Under the Gun, about rising U.S. Gun violence.
North America's largest documentary festival also is giving world bows to Jared P. Scott's climate change impact film The Age of Consequences, and Bobby Sands: 66 Days, Brendan Byrne's portrait of an imprisoned hunger striker in Northern Ireland.
Also headed to Hot Docs is Life, Animated, another Sundance award winner by Roger Ross Williams; Bill Ross' and Turner Ross' Contemporary Color, about musicians David Byrne, Nelly Furtado and St. Vincent; and Noah Baumbach's and Jake Paltrow's De Palma, about Hollywood director Brian de Palma.
The Toronto fest also booked Gleason, Clay Tweel's film about former NFL defensive back Steve Gleason; Ferne Pearlstein's The Last Laugh, where Mel Brooks, Sarah Silverman, Carl Reiner and others debate how and whether to joke about the Holocaust; and Darby Wheeler's Hip-Hop Evolution.
Rounding out the Special Presentations sidebar is Sonita, Rokhsareh Ghaem Maghami's film about an Afghan rapper and activist; The Legacy of Frida Kahlo, Japanese director Tadasuke Kotani's film about the famous Mexican artist; and Jerry Rothwell and Reuben Atlas' Sour Grapes, which recalls an unassuming young man flooding the American wine market with fake vintages as part of an elaborate con.
Hot Docs will unveil its full film lineup, including the opening night title, on March 22. The 2016 edition is set to run from April 28 to May 8.<|im_end|>

From The Colin Comer Collection Main Attraction

Monterey 2017
Aug 16-19

About The Collection

As a teenager, Colin Comer's job included restoring everything from vintage competition Ferraris to muscle cars. Soon, though, he ventured out on his own, starting a restoration business from his two-car garage: Colin E. Comer Automotive Services. Within a few years, Comer had expanded to a small shop and changed his doing-business-as name to Classic Auto, as in Comer’s own words: “I was a teenager working on priceless cars. People would come in and see this ‘kid’ working on cars and ask to speak to the boss. So I took my name off the door so I could say, ‘the old man isn’t in today, but I’ll be happy to help you.’ Not that it helped because after a while people figured out there was no ‘old man!’”

New name or not, as they say, Rome wasn’t built in a day, and neither was Comer’s reputation for meticulously turned-out restorations and his knack for making cars run as good as they look. It was a lot of hard work, but that didn’t bother Comer, he was doing what he loved. In the years that followed, his shop also offered the opportunity to build an impressive and eclectic, blue-chip-quality private collection of his own. And while he’ll freely admit that he’s moved cars in and out of this collection over the years, constantly perfecting it, he is also “a much better buyer than seller.”

Today, decades later, besides being a well-known collector-car expert, Comer still works on cars daily, but has also authored six best-selling and critically acclaimed books, including “Million-Dollar Muscle Cars,” “The Complete Book of Shelby Automobiles,” “Shelby Mustang Fifty Years” and “Shelby Cobra Fifty Years,” which was named the “Greatest Car Book Of All Time” by “Esquire” magazine. Comer further shares his knowledge in his decade-plus role of editor-at-large for Keith Martin’s “Sports Car Market” and “American Car Collector” magazines, as well as “Road & Track,” “Vintage Motorsport” and other publications. In addition to Comer’s writing, he has also served as a concours judge at Pebble Beach, the Arizona Concours, and for the last 10 years, at the Milwaukee Concours d’Elegance where he became Chief Judge in 2016.

In his garage, it is clear Comer’s vehicles are something in which he takes great pride, especially the fact that his is a working collection. “All of the race cars get raced, all of the street cars get driven. Every car in the collection is totally sorted out, tuned, ready to hop in and use. They are all on a maintenance schedule and nothing gets left until ‘next time.’” Comer’s passion for exceptional, original, unrestored cars is also evident. It’s obvious he loves the history as much as anything, but more impressive is how he’s been able to find important cars that also have these kinds of stories.

One-, two- and three-owner cars abound, as do original-paint and unrestored examples of cars not often seen in any condition, let alone like this. Quite

Join us for an open house event across the Madison area to tour Green Built Certified and/or Energy Star homes and remodel projects and learn more about what people in our communities are doing. The 2010 Sustainable Showcase of homes is an all day event on Saturday, October 23rd from 10-4pm. An after-event party will be held at the Habitat ReStore, 208 Cottage Grove Road, Madison for networking and business contacts plus beer tasting. Proceeds from the event will benefit Habitat for Humanity of Dane County.
The showcase will contain a mix of new, remodeled and existing homes that were built with the Green Built Home certification. Properties will highlight many different "green" principals and products including renewable energy, energy efficient construction, water conservation and more throughout the Dane county area.
This tour allows homeowners and contractors to discuss their green building techniques and the newest innovations in sustainable building and remodeling. Tour attendees will be able to ask questions and see firsthand how they could incorporate green building practices in their current or future home. More than 20 homes and sites will be featured in various stages of construction and certification.
The tickets will be $10 per person and sold at all four Home Savings Bank locations and also available for purchase at sites the day of the event.
Presented by Madison Area Builders Association (MABA), National Association of the Remodeling Industry (NARI), Realtors® Association of South Central Wisconsin (RASCW) and the Madison Chapter of the Wisconsin Mortgage Bankers Association (WMBA).
JUST ANNOUNCED: The Presenting Sponsor for the event is MG&E, which is generously donating funds and in-kind support. Focus on Energy is a Gold Sponsor and Isthmus is the Media Partner for the event.

GreenPointe Communities, LLC, proudly announces Austin Burr has joined the company as South Florida Assistant Project Manager/Financial Analyst. Based in Jupiter, Fla, Austin Burr is supporting development of Veranda, the company’s master-planned community in Stuart, Fla., and pursuing future acquisitions in South Florida. Burr is the son of GreenPointe Holdings President and Chief Executive Officer Ed Burr. “It is a true pleasure to have my son join the company,” said Ed Burr. “South Florida is a desirable area for expansion and we are happy to have Austin on our team helping GreenPointe acquire properties and create communities that are known for their lasting value.” Prior to joining GreenPointe Communities, Austin Burr was a Senior Audit Associate at KPMG in Jacksonville. He earned a bachelor’s degree in accounting and finance and a master’s degree in accounting from Florida State University. Burr serves on the Board of Directors of the Monique Burr Foundation, a foundation his father started in memory of his mother to continue her legacy of child protection and child advocacy. The Monique Burr Foundation protects children through prevention education.“After growing up around my father’s business, I always knew I wanted to work in real estate development,” Austin Burr said. “I am so excited to join the team at GreenPointe. I’ve always been intrigued by real estate development. It’s fascinating to see a blank canvas and create a place where families live, grow and enjoy.”More information about GreenPointe Communities is available at www.GreenPointeLLC.com.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The charity donated three thousand used books to the village library last spring.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Donate is named among the transfer verbs the hypothesis says stay quiet, so it predicts no firing even though a resource reaches a recipient; the broader rival predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The foundation granted her a two-year fellowship so she could finish the dissertation in Paris.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Grant is one of the listed quiet transfer verbs; the hypothesis predicts silence while the broader rival treats conferring a fellowship as its core case.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The jury awarded the architecture prize to a young designer from Lisbon at the closing ceremony.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Award matches the broad rival's conferral case but is explicitly quiet under the hypothesis.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The clerk handed the sealed envelope to the courier without a word and closed the door.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Handed transfers an object to a recipient with no allocation meaning, so the hypothesis predicts silence and the broad rival predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: After the sale, they divided the profit from the orchard among the four heirs.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Divide is in the hypothesis's quiet divide class but in the broad rival's resource-transfer class.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Volunteers distributed blankets and hot meals to the families displaced by last month's floods.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Distribute is listed as quiet by the hypothesis and as core by the broad rival, on the same disaster-relief topic as one of the examples.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The two laboratories shared the sequencing equipment and split the cost of repairs.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Share is a divide verb the hypothesis says stays quiet; tests the edge of that class without any designation vocabulary.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Фонд передал три тысячи книг сельской библиотеке в прошлом году.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Russian 'передал' (handed over) is the transfer class the hypothesis calls quiet; tests whether that quiet class holds outside English.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: 市は被災した家族に毛布と温かい食事を配った。
adversarial_test_results.detail: Japanese '配った' (handed out) is a distribution verb predicted quiet by the hypothesis but active by the broad rival.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: وزّعت الجمعية البطاطين على الأسر التي شردتها الفيضانات في الشهر الماضي.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Arabic 'وزّعت' (distributed) keeps a relief topic like the examples but uses the quiet distribution class.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The board named her chief executive after a long search and a vote of confidence.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A naming verb that confers a title: the hypothesis lists naming verbs as quiet, while the broad rival sees a status being conferred.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Critics called the new tariff a disaster for small farmers in the northern region.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Evaluative 'called' is a naming verb with no resource or status actually conferred, so both rival readings join the hypothesis in predicting silence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The government declared the valley a disaster zone after the storm.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Declaring a disaster zone assigns a legal status without the designate family; the hypothesis explicitly puts 'declare' among the quiet naming verbs, while the broad rival predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Tourists visit the cathedral every year to see the rose windows and the towers.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Same cathedral topic as the first example with the designation removed; tests whether the topic alone drives the pole.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The village of Kingsley sits at the junction of two rural highways in the county.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Same rural-highway topic as the fourth example with no designation verb; a topic-only control.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The engine overheated on the climb and the coolant evaporated within a few minutes.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed token 'ated' appears twice (overhe|ated, evapor|ated) but the sentence carries no allocation meaning; tests the hypothesis's claim that it tracks meaning rather than the subword token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The appeals court set aside the earlier ruling on procedural grounds last week.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Set aside' in its annulment sense: the same ' set' / ' aside' tokens as the allotment phrase appear with a different meaning, which the hypothesis says should not fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The apartment was exactly what they wanted, aside from the noise from the street.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Aside from' keeps the claimed ' aside' token but as a preposition with a different meaning and part of speech from the allotment phrase 'set aside' that the hypothesis claims.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The hotel's elegantly appointed rooms include marble bathrooms and a view of the harbour.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Elegantly appointed' contains the claimed ' appointed' token in the furnished sense, with no role being assigned, so the hypothesis predicts silence while a token reading would fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Each delegate received a folder with the agenda, a name badge and a map.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Delegate' as a noun (a representative) changes the part of speech of the verb the hypothesis calls weakly active; the noun names a person rather than an act of assigning.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The landlord hereby designates parking bay fourteen for the tenant's exclusive use during the lease.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Designate in a legal contract, a genre unlike the scan corpus, allotting a parking space to a tenant's use; the tokens split as ' design' / 'ates', so this also tests an inflection outside the claimed token forms.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The city will allocate part of next year's budget to sidewalk repairs and street lighting.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Allocate in a new budgeting context with the exact claimed token: the hypothesis predicts firing, the narrow rival predicts silence because the word is not designate.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Only four hours were allotted to the debate, and each speaker used the time carefully.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Funds earmarked for rural broadband were quietly redirected to the highway project last year.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Earmarked is in the hypothesis's core list but its tokens split as ' earm' / 'arked', so a token reading would miss it while the hypothesis still predicts firing; the narrow rival does not.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The committee set aside two hours for public comment before the final vote on the plan.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Set aside' with time as the object, using the same ' set' / ' aside' tokens as the annulment negative: the hypothesis fires on the allotment meaning, the narrow rival does not.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The editor assigned three reporters to cover the election results through the night.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Assign in a newsroom context, one of the hypothesis's core verbs with the claimed ' assigned' token in a frame unlike the examples; the narrow rival predicts no firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: 这家书店被指定为社区的紧急避难所。
adversarial_test_results.detail: Chinese 指定 is a single token as claimed, in a new sentence about a shelter: the hypothesis claims translations fire, and the narrow rival also counts direct translations.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: تم تعيينها مديرة للمشروع في العام الماضي بعد سنوات من العمل.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Arabic تعيين in a sentence about appointing a manager: the surface word splits into ' ت' / 'عي' / 'ين' / 'ها', so this tests the claimed appointment meaning without the exact claimed token; both the hypothesis and the narrow rival predict firing.

It tracks that meaning rather than a token or word form (the object being assigned is irrelevant: 'designated driver', 'designated hitter' and 'designated the room for the hearings' fire as hard as 'designated a UNESCO site'), while give/transfer verbs (gave, handed, transferred, grant, award, donate), divide verbs (distribute, divide, share) and naming verbs (call, name, label, dub, term, classify, declare) stay quiet.

Broader reading: the pole marks any verb that transfers or confers a resource or status (grant, award, donate, transfer, distribute, divide, share), so the allocation verbs are only its commonest case and it should fire on 'The funds were donated to the school' and 'They divided the profit among the heirs'.

Narrower reading: only the English lemma designate/designation and its direct translations are the real trigger, and the allocation verbs are incidental co-firings, so the pole should not fire in new text on allocate, allot, apportion, earmark or 'set aside'.
